thinkers.name: Sam Altman

roles.title: CEO (briefly removed by the board Nov 2023, reinstated days later)

thinkers.bio: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, which launched ChatGPT in Nov 2022 and turned large language models into a mass-market product. Uses his blog to publish AI forecasts and policy positions, and has led the industry's largest compute-financing push.

influence: Shapes public and policy narratives (AGI framing, licensing proposal, compute-cost 'observations') more than the technical research agenda.
foresight: Several directional calls held up, such as falling cost per capability and mainstream legal and medical use. Dated agent and superintelligence calls ran early or are still open.
allocation: Directs OpenAI capital, including the Microsoft partnership, Stargate and about $1.4T of stated compute commitments.
contribution: Led ChatGPT commercialization, the largest consumer AI product of the period.
corpus: Dated essays (2021 to 2025), testimony and frequent interviews. Much of it mixes personal forecasts with corporate positioning.
future: OpenAI's scale and compute commitments make his decisions central to the ecosystem through the end of the decade.

mentalModel.summary: As YC president and OpenAI co-founder (Dec 2015), he treated AGI as a long-horizon but real possibility. He co-founded OpenAI as a nonprofit counterweight to concentrated corporate AI.
Concluded that AGI would need huge capital and compute. In 2019 he restructured OpenAI into a capped-profit entity and took Microsoft's $1B investment.

In 'Moore's Law for Everything' (Mar 2021) he forecast thinking programs within five years that could read legal documents and give medical advice. He argued that the resulting shift from labor to capital needed redistribution through taxes on companies and land.

After ChatGPT, he asked Congress for a licensing agency for models above a capability threshold (May 2023) and signed the CAIS extinction-risk statement. He presented safety and scaling as compatible.
Framed deep learning as having 'worked' and predicted superintelligence possibly within 'a few thousand days' (Sep 2024). His rhetoric moved from risk toward abundance.

Declared confidence in knowing how to build AGI, predicted agents joining the workforce in 2025, and said AI cost falls about 10x per year. He reversed on open weights (gpt-oss) and committed about $1.4T to compute.

No new 2026 Altman essay was verified this session. Reported outcomes (run-rate near $70B in Sep 2026, AI-credited Erdős-problem solutions) bear on his 2025 forecasts, but his own 2026 statements were not captured.

reversals.from: Closed frontier weights; OpenAI had released no open-weight LLM since GPT-2 (2019).
reversals.to: Said OpenAI had been on the 'wrong side of history' on open source. OpenAI then released the gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b open-weight models (Aug 2025).
reversals.trigger: DeepSeek's open-weight releases. Altman said DeepSeek had lessened OpenAI's lead.

reversals.to: Capped-profit structure with large corporate investment (Microsoft, 2019). OpenAI later recapitalized into a public benefit corporation (Oct 2025).
reversals.trigger: Belief that frontier compute costs could not be met with philanthropy.

reversals.from: Called for a federal licensing agency for capable models (May 2023).
reversals.to: Recalled: in May 2025 Senate testimony he warned that requiring government pre-approval for model releases would be harmful, and favored light-touch federal rules.
reversals.trigger: Competition with China and a changed US political climate (recalled; not re-verified this session).

Quotes come from search-snippet reproductions in secondary coverage. Altman's forecasts are often hedged ('may', 'likely') and are hard to separate from OpenAI marketing and fundraising.

thinkers.name: Dario Amodei
thinkers.bio: Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic, and earlier OpenAI's VP of Research during GPT-2 and GPT-3. He co-authored the 2020 scaling-laws paper and is among the most explicit near-term forecasters of 'powerful AI' and its labor impact.

influence: Co-authored the scaling-laws work and the 'big blob of compute' thesis, and co-founded the 'safety lab at the frontier' model.
foresight: His scaling bet was early and right. His coding and labor forecasts are specific but ran early, or remain open.
allocation: Leads Anthropic, whose run-rate was reported at about $19B in early 2026.
contribution: Shaped GPT-2 and GPT-3 at OpenAI. Claude models, including Claude Code, became leading coding systems.
corpus: Long dated essays (Machines of Loving Grace, The Urgency of Interpretability, the DeepSeek and export-controls essay) plus many interviews with explicit dates.
future: A frontier lab CEO who also shapes export-control and safety policy.

mentalModel.summary: Moved from biophysics into deep learning at Baidu (Deep Speech 2) and Google Brain. He co-authored 'Concrete Problems in AI Safety' (2016), treating safety as an empirical ML problem.
Held the 'big blob of compute' view: capability comes mostly from scaling compute and data with simple objectives. He led research at OpenAI through GPT-2.
Co-authored the power-law scaling results (Jan 2020) and the GPT-3 paper. He left OpenAI to found Anthropic (2021) as a safety-focused lab that would still compete at the frontier.
Forecast human-level conversational AI within two to three years (Aug 2023). He signed the CAIS statement and pushed responsible scaling policies.
In 'Machines of Loving Grace' (Oct 2024) he described a 'country of geniuses in a datacenter' possibly arriving as early as 2026. He also described a 'compressed 21st century' of scientific progress.

Pressed hardest of any lab CEO on concrete short-term forecasts: AI writing 90% of code within 3 to 6 months, and half of entry-level white-collar jobs at risk. He backed export controls against China and urged interpretability by 2027.
Recalled, low confidence: an essay in Jan 2026 ('The Adolescence of Technology') restated near-term powerful-AI risks. In a Feb 2026 dispute he held to limits on military uses of Claude.

reversals.from: Led research at OpenAI and championed GPT-2 and GPT-3 scaling inside it.
reversals.to: Left with colleagues to found Anthropic as a separate safety-focused lab.
reversals.trigger: Reported disagreements over safety priorities and commercialization at OpenAI. His public explanation was a different approach to safety, not a single stated grievance.

reversals.from: Early Anthropic messaging (2022 to 2023, as reported) suggested the lab would avoid advancing the capability frontier.
reversals.to: Released models marketed as state of the art (Claude 3, 2024) and competed head-on at the frontier.
reversals.trigger: Commercial competition and the 'race to the top' rationale. Recalled; the investor-deck reporting was not re-verified this session.

All Amodei evidence is recalled, not re-confirmed, and is marked verbatim=false. The dates and wording of the CFR (Mar 2025) and Axios (May 2025) remarks are from memory. His forecasts are often explicitly hedged ('could', 'may'), and this file keeps those hedges.

thinkers.name: Demis Hassabis
thinkers.bio: Neuroscientist and co-founder of DeepMind (AlphaGo, AlphaFold), now CEO of Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs. He shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold.

influence: His AlphaGo and AlphaFold work defined deep RL and AI-for-science agendas.
foresight: His long-running AI-for-science thesis was vindicated by AlphaFold and the Nobel. His AGI timelines are comparatively measured.
allocation: Steers Google's frontier model effort (Gemini) and Isomorphic Labs.
contribution: AlphaGo, AlphaFold, and the Gemini program.
corpus: Many talks and interviews, but few dated, falsifiable forecasts; most are ranges like '5 to 10 years'.
future: Leads one of the two or three best-resourced frontier labs.

mentalModel.summary: Mission: 'solve intelligence, then use it to solve everything else'. His route was neuroscience-inspired deep reinforcement learning (Atari DQN, AlphaGo), and he accepted Google's 2014 acquisition to get resources.
Treated games as stepping stones toward general learning (AlphaZero) and turned toward scientific problems such as protein folding.
AlphaFold 2 (CASP14, 2020; Nature, 2021) showed AI could solve a 50-year-old scientific problem. He spun out Isomorphic Labs for drug discovery.
Signed the CAIS extinction-risk statement and called for international oversight bodies (IPCC/CERN-like). He merged Brain and DeepMind into Google DeepMind to compete in generative AI.
Warned that generative-AI investment carried crypto-like hype, while holding that AI was underhyped long-term. He received the Nobel Prize for AlphaFold.

Put AGI at roughly 5 to 10 years away and said scaling is necessary but may need one or two more breakthroughs, such as world models and consistency. He forecast AI-designed drugs entering clinical trials by end-2025.
No dated 2026 Hassabis statements were verified this session.

reversals.from: DeepMind ran as a research-first unit with limited productization and kept its distance from Google Brain.
reversals.to: Merged with Brain into Google DeepMind, a product-driven organization shipping Gemini against OpenAI.
reversals.trigger: ChatGPT's launch and competitive pressure on Google (recalled).

thinkers.corpusNotes: The search budget ran out before any Hassabis-specific query, so all evidence except the canonical Nature and Nobel pages is recalled and marked verbatim=false. His forecasts are mostly ranges with caveats, which limits falsifiability.

thinkers.name: Elon Musk
thinkers.bio: CEO of Tesla, co-founder and early funder of OpenAI, and founder of xAI (Grok). He is one of the most prominent voices on AI existential risk and one of the most prolific makers of missed autonomy deadlines.

influence: Popularized AI existential-risk concerns early (2014) but contributed little to the research agenda.
foresight: His self-driving, robotaxi, AGI and Optimus deadlines have repeatedly been missed.
allocation: Controls very large capital flows: Tesla autonomy, xAI's Colossus clusters, and the 2015 OpenAI funding.
contribution: Built Tesla's vision-based driving stack and quickly built xAI's frontier compute (Colossus).
corpus: Huge volume of tweets and calls with dated forecasts, but inconsistent and often promotional.
future: xAI compute scale, robotaxis and Optimus give him leverage, though his record lowers his credibility.

mentalModel.summary: Called AI the biggest existential threat ('summoning the demon', 2014) and co-founded OpenAI (2015) as a nonprofit counterweight to Google/DeepMind.
Called for proactive AI regulation (2017) while promising imminent full self-driving. He left the OpenAI board in Feb 2018.
Kept promising robotaxis within a year and pursued vision-only, end-to-end driving at Tesla.
Signed the March 2023 pause letter, then founded xAI in July 2023 to build 'maximally truth-seeking' AI.
Sued OpenAI for abandoning its open, nonprofit mission and released Grok-1 weights. He predicted AGI smarter than the smartest human by 2025 or 2026 and built the 100k-GPU Colossus.
Led a $97.4B bid for control of OpenAI and launched the Austin robotaxi pilot. He forecast robotaxi coverage of about half the US population and thousands of Optimus robots by end-2025.
No dated 2026 Musk statements were verified this session. The status of the OpenAI litigation and of robotaxis as of Oct 2026 was not verified.

reversals.from: Signed the March 2023 open letter calling on labs to pause training of systems more powerful than GPT-4 for six months.
reversals.to: Founded xAI four months later and raced to build frontier models (Grok) and the largest GPU clusters.
reversals.trigger: Stated desire for a 'truth-seeking' alternative to OpenAI and Google. Competitive motives were widely inferred.

reversals.from: Co-founder, co-chair and major early donor of OpenAI (2015 to 2018).
reversals.to: Plaintiff suing OpenAI and Altman for breaching the founding nonprofit and open mission, and later bidder to take control (Feb 2025).
reversals.trigger: OpenAI's capped-profit and Microsoft partnership path and its for-profit restructuring.

His forecasts often come in earnings calls and tweets alongside marketing, so personal belief and promotion are hard to separate.

thinkers.name: Mustafa Suleyman

roles.title: VP, AI product management and policy

thinkers.bio: Co-founder of DeepMind and Inflection AI (Pi), now CEO of Microsoft AI responsible for Copilot and MAI models. He wrote 'The Coming Wave' (2023) on AI containment and the 2025 'seemingly conscious AI' warning.

influence: Shaped governance discourse (containment, the 'modern Turing test', seemingly conscious AI) more than technical direction.
foresight: His dated near-term calls (hallucinations solved by 2025, $100k to $1M ACI within about two years) appear premature. His longer-term calls are open.
allocation: Directs Microsoft's consumer AI and in-house model effort, within Microsoft's broader OpenAI-dependent strategy.
contribution: Co-founded DeepMind and built Pi and Microsoft Copilot consumer products.
corpus: A book, essays and many interviews with some dated forecasts.
future: Microsoft's in-house superintelligence effort gives him influence, but less than at the leading labs.

mentalModel.summary: Co-founded DeepMind and led applied AI, including DeepMind Health. He believed AI could be deployed quickly in public services, a stance tested by the 2017 ICO ruling on NHS data.
Focused on applied AI and ethics inside DeepMind and Google. Few dated public forecasts were found for this period.

Founded Inflection to build a personal AI for everyone (Pi). He predicted hallucinations would be largely fixed by 2025 and proposed the $100k-to-$1M 'modern Turing test' for artificial capable intelligence. In 'The Coming Wave' he argued containment is not possible but must be.
Joined Microsoft (Mar 2024) as Inflection's independent path ended. In a TED talk he described AI as a 'new digital species'.

Warned that 'seemingly conscious AI' could arrive in 2 to 3 years and that labs should not build AI that presents as a person. He launched a 'humanist superintelligence' team after Microsoft won freedom to pursue AGI independently.
Recalled, low confidence: in Feb 2026 he forecast that most white-collar professional tasks would be automated within 12 to 18 months.

reversals.from: Independent startup strategy: Inflection raised $1.3B in 2023 to build its own frontier models and the Pi assistant.
reversals.to: Joined Microsoft with most of Inflection's staff, and Inflection pivoted to enterprise.
reversals.trigger: Frontier-scale capital needs and weak consumer traction for Pi (recalled).

reversals.from: Built Pi as an empathetic, emotionally engaging personal AI companion (2023).
reversals.to: Argued labs should not build AI that seems conscious or encourages attachment, warning of 'psychosis risk'.
reversals.trigger: Reports of user over-attachment and 'AI psychosis', and the emerging 'model welfare' debate. The framing as a reversal is this analyst's interpretation.

assertions.claim: Restructured OpenAI from a nonprofit into a capped-profit entity and took Microsoft's $1B investment, betting that AGI requires capital and compute at a scale philanthropy cannot supply.
assumptions: Capability keeps scaling with compute
Products funded by frontier models can generate revenue to finance more compute
assertions.predictedOutcome: OpenAI would need, and be able to raise, multi-billion-dollar capital through commercial products and a hyperscaler partner.
assertions.contextAtTime: In 2019, GPT-2 had just been released; the scaling-laws paper was not yet published, and few labs spent at this scale.
assertions.outcome: OpenAI raised far larger sums (Microsoft about $13B; Stargate), reported an annualized revenue run rate of about $50B to $70B by Sep 2026, and recapitalized as a public benefit corporation in Oct 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: The implied belief that frontier AI is capital-intensive and commercially fundable was borne out, and early. In 2019 it was a minority bet; profitability and governance costs remain unresolved.
assertions.evolution: Extended through the Oct 2025 recapitalization and about $1.4T of compute commitments.

assertions.claim: In the next five years, computer programs that can think will read legal documents and give medical advice.
assumptions: Language-model capability keeps improving with scale
Users and institutions are willing to rely on AI for professional-domain tasks
assertions.predictedOutcome: By about 2026, AI systems routinely read legal documents and give medical advice.
assertions.contextAtTime: GPT-3 (2020) was impressive but unreliable; few experts expected mainstream professional use within five years.
assertions.outcome: By 2023 to 2026, LLM assistants were widely used to review legal documents and answer medical questions. Professional-standard autonomous advice without human oversight was not established, and 'can think' remains contested.
assertions.verdictRationale: The surface behavior (reading legal documents, giving medical advice) was widely achieved within the window, starting with GPT-4 in 2023, which was bold for 2021. Trackers disagree only on whether advice meets a professional standard.
assertions.evolution: No revision found; later essays (2024 to 2025) generalized it into broader AGI and superintelligence claims.

assertions.claim: If AI-driven wealth is taxed through company equity and land (an 'American Equity Fund'), it could pay every US adult about $13,500 a year within 10 years. AI will shift wealth from labor to capital.
assumptions: AI drives very rapid GDP and asset growth
Political adoption of new wealth taxes
assertions.predictedOutcome: By about 2031, AI-generated wealth could fund about $13,500 per adult per year if the proposed taxes were adopted.
assertions.contextAtTime: A 2021 pre-ChatGPT policy essay; UBI was a niche topic.
assertions.outcome: No such fund exists. AI has concentrated value in a few companies, and general goods (housing, healthcare, education) have not followed a 'Moore's Law' decline. The horizon has not been reached.
assertions.verdictRationale: This is conditional on a policy that was not adopted, and the 2031 horizon has not passed.
assertions.evolution: Altman later floated 'universal basic compute' ideas (2024, recalled) instead of the equity-fund design.

assertions.claim: Proposed that the US (or a global body) license AI models above a capability threshold, with testing requirements and independent audits, and a regulator able to revoke licenses.
assumptions: Capability thresholds can be defined and measured
A regulator can keep pace with frontier labs
assertions.predictedOutcome: A licensing regime for frontier models would reduce catastrophic risk without stopping progress.
assertions.contextAtTime: Six months after ChatGPT, there was bipartisan appetite for AI regulation, and Gary Marcus testified alongside him in favor of licensing. Critics saw regulatory-capture motives.
assertions.outcome: No US federal licensing agency was created. The 2023 executive order's reporting rules were rescinded in Jan 2025, and Altman later argued against pre-approval regimes (recalled).
assertions.verdictRationale: A normative policy proposal, not a forecast. It was not adopted, and its merits cannot be falsified.
assertions.evolution: Softened by 2025: he favored light-touch federal rules and warned against pre-approval (recalled, ev-altman-17).

assertions.claim: It is possible that we will have superintelligence in 'a few thousand days (!); it may take longer, but I'm confident we'll get there.'
assumptions: Deep learning keeps scaling predictably
Sufficient compute and energy are built
assertions.predictedOutcome: Superintelligence within roughly 5 to 15 years of Sep 2024 (a few thousand days), hedged as 'possible'.
assertions.horizon: a few thousand days from Sep 2024 (about 2030 to 2035)
assertions.contextAtTime: o1 reasoning models had just been previewed. Pretraining returns were being debated, and many researchers (LeCun, Marcus) disputed near-term superintelligence.
assertions.outcome: As of Oct 2026, no system was broadly recognized as superintelligent, though frontier models showed expert-level performance in narrow domains (competition math, coding).
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached, and the claim was hedged as 'possible'.
assertions.evolution: Reinforced in Reflections (Jan 2025) and The Gentle Singularity (Jun 2025), which said 'we are past the event horizon'.

assertions.claim: In 2025, we may see the first AI agents 'join the workforce' and materially change the output of companies.
assumptions: Agent reliability is good enough for unsupervised multi-step work
Enterprises integrate agents into workflows within a year
assertions.predictedOutcome: During 2025, some companies deploy AI agents that materially change their output.
assertions.contextAtTime: Agents (Operator, early coding agents) were demos at the start of 2025, and reliability on long tasks was poor.
assertions.outcome: Coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor agents) were widely adopted in 2025. McKinsey found 62% of firms experimenting with agents but no more than 10% scaling them in any function, and only 39% reporting any enterprise EBIT impact from AI. Karpathy called 2025 the start of a 'decade of agents'.
assertions.verdictRationale: The hedged 'may see the first' was met in software engineering, where agents materially changed output at some firms. Broad workforce integration with measured output change had not happened by end-2025.
assertions.evolution: In The Gentle Singularity (Jun 2025) he said 2025 had seen agents doing real cognitive work, especially code.

assertions.claim: The cost to use a given level of AI falls about 10x every 12 months, and lower prices lead to much more use.
assumptions: Algorithmic efficiency, distillation and hardware improvements continue
Demand is highly price-elastic (Jevons effect)
assertions.predictedOutcome: The price for a fixed capability level keeps falling about 10x per year, and total usage and spend rise.
assertions.contextAtTime: He cited the roughly 150x drop in per-token price from GPT-4 (early 2023) to GPT-4o (mid-2024), and DeepSeek-V3 and R1 had just shown cheap near-frontier models.
assertions.outcome: Per-token prices for fixed capability kept falling steeply through 2025 to 2026 (GPT-5 family, gpt-oss, Chinese open-weight models). Total spend rose sharply: OpenAI run rate went from above $20B at end-2025 to a reported $50B to $70B in Sep 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: Both halves (rapid price decline per capability and rising total usage) were consistent with the data available. The exact 10x rate varies by capability threshold.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: 2026 will likely see the arrival of systems that can figure out novel insights.
assumptions: Reasoning and RL scaling keeps improving
Novel insights can be verified (math proofs, experiments)
assertions.predictedOutcome: During 2026, AI systems produce verifiably new scientific or mathematical results.
assertions.contextAtTime: Scientists were sceptical (TechCrunch). Reasoning models had shown competition-level math but no accepted original research results.
assertions.outcome: By early 2026, GPT-5.2 models were credited in Terence Tao's Erdős-problems database with complete solutions to problems #205 and #652, with no prior literature found. A Nov 2025 OpenAI paper collected cases of GPT-5 contributing new research steps. A walked-back Oct 2025 claim shows the evidence needs care.
assertions.verdictRationale: Verifiable, modest novel math results arrived in the predicted window. The significance of the insights is debated and the year is not over, so this is provisional.
assertions.evolution: No revision found; the 2027 robotics step of the same schedule is unresolved.

assertions.claim: Committed OpenAI to about 30 GW of compute (about $1.4T over roughly 8 years) and set an aspiration to add 1 GW of compute per week.
assumptions: Demand for AI keeps growing fast enough to service the commitments
Capital markets keep financing at high valuations
Scaling compute keeps yielding more valuable models
assertions.predictedOutcome: Revenue grows into hundreds of billions to justify the commitments, and capacity is built on schedule.
assertions.contextAtTime: OpenAI was about to exceed $20B annualized revenue (end-2025). Analysts questioned financing, and some (for example David Cahn's '$600B question') had flagged an AI capex-revenue gap.
assertions.outcome: By Sep 2026, OpenAI's reported run rate was about $50B (Bloomberg) to nearly $70B (Axios), and it was reportedly raising at least $30B at about a $1.4T valuation. The commitments are mostly still ahead.
assertions.verdictRationale: This is a multi-year bet. Revenue has grown fast, but nowhere near the scale needed to cover $1.4T, so it is not yet judgeable.
assertions.evolution: Escalated from the $500B Stargate announcement (Jan 2025).

assertions.claim: Language-model performance improves as a smooth power law in model size, data and compute. Scaling these up (the 'big blob of compute') is the main driver of capability.
assumptions: Power laws continue beyond the measured range
Enough data and compute can be obtained
assertions.predictedOutcome: Larger models trained with more compute will be predictably more capable, which justifies orders-of-magnitude compute increases.
assertions.contextAtTime: In 2020 most of the field doubted that scale alone would yield general capabilities; GPT-3 had not yet been released.
assertions.outcome: Scaling drove GPT-3, GPT-4, Claude and Gemini capability gains through 2024. From 2024 to 2025, gains increasingly came from RL and inference-time scaling as well as pretraining, and pretraining returns were debated.
assertions.verdictRationale: A contrarian, empirically grounded bet that defined the industry's strategy for five years. It was refined, not refuted, by later reasoning-scaling.
assertions.evolution: From 2024 to 2025 he extended the thesis to RL and test-time compute.

assertions.claim: Co-founded Anthropic: a safety-focused lab must itself build frontier models to do relevant safety research and set norms (a 'race to the top').
assumptions: Safety research needs frontier-scale models
A safety brand can be commercially competitive
assertions.predictedOutcome: Anthropic stays at the frontier while influencing industry safety norms.
assertions.contextAtTime: OpenAI had just signed with Microsoft; there were few independent frontier labs.
assertions.outcome: Claude models were among the frontier leaders, especially in coding. Anthropic's run rate was reported at about $19B in early 2026. Responsible-scaling-style policies were adopted by other labs.
assertions.verdictRationale: The commercial viability of a safety-branded frontier lab was demonstrated. Whether it actually improved safety outcomes is not measurable.
assertions.evolution: Accepted Gulf sovereign investment (2025, recalled) and pushed the frontier, so critics saw convergence with competitors.

assertions.claim: A model that, over an hour of conversation, seems like a generally well-educated human could be two or three years away.
assumptions: Continued scaling of pretraining and post-training
assertions.predictedOutcome: By about 2025 to 2026, conversational models are indistinguishable from an educated human in casual hour-long conversation.
assertions.contextAtTime: GPT-4 and Claude 2 were fluent but error-prone. Most forecasters placed robust human-level conversation further out.
assertions.outcome: By 2025, frontier models (GPT-4.5, Claude 3.7/4, Gemini 2.5) were judged human in controlled Turing-test studies (recalled: a 2025 UCSD study found GPT-4.5 judged human more often than humans) and were widely used as general assistants. Agentic economic autonomy, which he did not claim, remained limited.
assertions.verdictRationale: The narrow, explicitly scoped claim (conversational generalist) was met within the window. He explicitly did not claim economic transformation.
assertions.evolution: Upgraded to the 'powerful AI as early as 2026' claim (Oct 2024).

assertions.claim: 'Powerful AI' (smarter than Nobel laureates across most fields, a 'country of geniuses in a datacenter') could come as early as 2026, though it could take much longer.
assumptions: Scaling of pretraining and RL continues
Autonomous long-horizon task ability emerges
Enough compute is available
assertions.predictedOutcome: Earliest case: systems meeting his powerful-AI definition exist in 2026, with a central expectation around 2026 to 2027.
assertions.horizon: as early as 2026; possibly much longer
assertions.contextAtTime: Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1-preview had just been released, and AI scientific discovery was not yet demonstrated.
assertions.outcome: As of Oct 2026, no system was widely accepted as meeting the powerful-AI definition (Nobel-level across fields, autonomous multi-week work). Models produced modest novel math results and strong coding agents.
assertions.verdictRationale: 'As early as 2026' was the optimistic edge of a hedged range. The central window (2026 to 2027) is not over, but the earliest case looks unlikely to be met in 2026.
assertions.evolution: Repeated through 2025, with talk of 2026 to 2027 at Davos 2025 (recalled), and in the Jan 2026 essay (recalled, low confidence).

assertions.claim: DeepSeek-V3's low training cost was roughly on the expected cost-reduction curve, not a unique breakthrough. Strict US chip export controls are decisive for keeping a US-led (unipolar) AI world around 2026 to 2027.
assumptions: Compute remains the binding constraint for frontier AI
Export controls can be enforced against smuggling
assertions.predictedOutcome: With tight controls, Chinese labs stay behind the frontier; without them, they reach parity.
assertions.contextAtTime: DeepSeek R1 had triggered a market selloff and a narrative that cheap training made compute less important. Nvidia (Huang) opposed controls.
assertions.outcome: Compute demand did not collapse, and hyperscaler capex rose. US policy shifted toward allowing some Nvidia sales to China (H20 in 2025 and later H200, recalled), while Chinese open-weight models stayed close behind the frontier.
assertions.verdictRationale: His cost-curve reading of DeepSeek fit the evidence and the compute-demand collapse narrative proved wrong. The policy counterfactual (controls being decisive) cannot be tested because the controls were loosened.
assertions.evolution: Continued advocacy into 2025 to 2026; a public clash with Huang (Jun 2025).

assertions.claim: In three to six months AI will be writing 90% of the code, and in 12 months we may be in a world where AI writes essentially all of the code.
assumptions: Coding agents improve rapidly
Developers adopt agentic tools at scale
Code volume, not human design work, is what is measured
assertions.predictedOutcome: By about Sep 2025, 90% of new code is AI-written; by about Mar 2026, nearly all.
assertions.contextAtTime: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and early Claude Code were just out. Google said about 25% of its new code was AI-generated (Oct 2024).
assertions.outcome: At Anthropic itself, leaders reported roughly 70 to 90% of code written by Claude by late 2025. Industry-wide shares were lower: Microsoft about 20 to 30% (Apr 2025) and Google at least 25 to 30%. 'Essentially all code' was not reached industry-wide by Mar 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: The directional bet (rapid shift to AI-written code) was right, and it came true inside frontier labs. As a general claim on his stated timeline, it overshot.
assertions.evolution: Later framed as true 'at Anthropic' and in some teams (recalled), narrowing the scope.

assertions.claim: AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10 to 20% within the next one to five years.
assumptions: Agents become reliable for routine knowledge work
Firms substitute rather than augment
Policy does not offset displacement
assertions.predictedOutcome: By 2026 to 2030, a large decline in entry-level white-collar employment and US unemployment of 10 to 20%.
assertions.contextAtTime: Unemployment was about 4%. Anecdotal reports of hiring freezes for juniors existed but there was little hard data. Huang publicly rejected the warning.
assertions.outcome: Early signals: a Stanford study (Aug 2025) found a 13% relative employment decline for 22-to-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations. The Yale Budget Lab (Oct 2025) found no broad occupational disruption. Aggregate US unemployment stayed far below 10% through the data available (2026 labor data not verified this session).
assertions.verdictRationale: The window runs to 2030 and was framed as 'could'. Early entry-level effects are consistent in direction, but the aggregate unemployment component shows no sign yet.
assertions.evolution: He repeated the warning through 2025 and proposed measures such as a 'token tax' (recalled).

assertions.claim: Goal: by 2027 interpretability should be able to reliably detect most model problems (an 'MRI for AI'). This is a race against capabilities that may reach a 'country of geniuses' first.
assumptions: Mechanistic interpretability scales to frontier models
Labs invest enough
assertions.predictedOutcome: By 2027, interpretability tools can reliably diagnose most model problems.
assertions.contextAtTime: Anthropic had published dictionary-learning features (2024) and circuit tracing (2025), and interpretability was still far from diagnostic use.
assertions.outcome: Interpretability research progressed, and Anthropic reported using it in pre-deployment audits (recalled). No field-wide reliable diagnostic exists as of Oct 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: This is a self-set goal with a 2027 deadline.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Kept Anthropic's usage limits barring Claude's use for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, even at the cost of a confrontation with the US Department of Defense.
assumptions: Usage restrictions are enforceable and matter for safety
Commercial and political costs are survivable
assertions.predictedOutcome: Anthropic keeps its restrictions despite losing some government business.
assertions.contextAtTime: Frontier labs were competing for national-security contracts (about $200M each in 2025, recalled).
assertions.outcome: Recalled: the administration ordered agencies off Anthropic and labelled it a supply-chain risk, and Anthropic contested this. The final status as of Oct 2026 was not verified.
assertions.verdictRationale: A values-driven action whose consequences were still playing out, and the facts could not be verified this session.
assertions.evolution: Consistent with the 2025 'Urgency of Interpretability' and earlier safety commitments.

assertions.claim: DeepMind's mission: solve intelligence, then use it to solve everything else, via general-purpose learning systems inspired by neuroscience and reinforcement learning.
assumptions: General learning algorithms exist and can be found
Large resources (Google) are available
assertions.predictedOutcome: General AI that then accelerates science across domains.
assertions.contextAtTime: Deep learning was newly practical (AlexNet 2012, DQN 2013), and AGI as a stated corporate goal was fringe.
assertions.outcome: DeepMind delivered AlphaGo, AlphaFold (Nobel 2024) and Gemini. 'Solve intelligence' remains unachieved, and the general path that worked was transformer scaling rather than the RL-first approach.
assertions.verdictRationale: An open-ended mission statement. The science-acceleration half is partly vindicated.
assertions.evolution: Kept the mission, but adopted LLM scaling (Gemini) as the main path after 2023.

assertions.claim: Deep neural networks combined with tree search and self-play reinforcement learning can master Go, a domain considered intractable for brute-force search.
assumptions: Learned value and policy functions generalize across Go positions
assertions.predictedOutcome: AlphaGo beats top professionals years ahead of expert expectations.
assertions.contextAtTime: Experts commonly estimated superhuman Go was about a decade away.
assertions.outcome: AlphaGo beat Fan Hui (2015) and Lee Sedol 4-1 (Mar 2016). AlphaZero generalized the approach (2017), and search plus learned evaluation influenced later reasoning-model research.
assertions.verdictRationale: Achieved well ahead of consensus expectations at the time.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: AI can solve fundamental scientific problems such as protein structure prediction and become a primary tool for scientific discovery.
assumptions: Rich structured datasets (PDB) and strong inductive biases
Problem has clear evaluation (CASP)
assertions.predictedOutcome: AI achieves near-experimental accuracy on protein folding and is adopted by biologists.
assertions.contextAtTime: Protein folding had been an unsolved 50-year challenge, and CASP progress was incremental before AlphaFold 1 (2018).
assertions.outcome: AlphaFold 2 reached near-experimental accuracy at CASP14, released over 200M structures, and earned Hassabis and Jumper the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
assertions.verdictRationale: Demonstrated and independently recognized by the Nobel committee.
assertions.evolution: Extended to drug discovery (Isomorphic) and AlphaFold 3 (2024).

assertions.claim: AI risk should be treated as seriously as the climate crisis, with an IPCC-like scientific body and CERN- or IAEA-like international institutions. Extinction risk should be a global priority.
assumptions: International coordination is feasible
Risks are serious enough to justify oversight
assertions.predictedOutcome: Creation of international scientific and oversight institutions for frontier AI.
assertions.contextAtTime: Ahead of the Bletchley AI Safety Summit, shortly after the CAIS statement.
assertions.outcome: National AI safety institutes and an International AI Safety Report (chaired by Bengio, 2025) emerged. No binding IAEA-like body exists, and US policy shifted toward deregulation in 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: A normative proposal, only partially institutionalized.
assertions.evolution: Continued to call for international standards in 2025 (recalled).

assertions.claim: The billions flowing into generative-AI startups bring crypto-like hype and some grifting. AI is overhyped in the short term but underhyped in the long term.
assumptions: Valuations are running ahead of near-term product value
assertions.predictedOutcome: Some AI startup valuations will deflate, while long-run impact exceeds expectations.
assertions.contextAtTime: Early 2024 saw a funding boom for LLM wrappers and model startups.
assertions.outcome: Several 2023-vintage model startups were absorbed (Inflection into Microsoft, Character.ai into a Google license, Adept into Amazon), while frontier-lab valuations and capex kept rising through Oct 2026 with no broad crash.
assertions.verdictRationale: Partly borne out for second-tier startups. The overall hype claim is not falsifiable yet.
assertions.evolution: Repeated the bubble-in-parts framing in 2025 (recalled).

assertions.claim: Expects the first AI-designed drugs from Isomorphic Labs to be in clinical trials by the end of 2025.
assumptions: AI-designed candidates pass preclinical work
Regulatory filings proceed on schedule
assertions.predictedOutcome: At least one Isomorphic AI-designed drug enters human clinical trials by Dec 2025.
assertions.contextAtTime: Several other AI-discovered molecules (for example Insilico's) were already in trials, and Isomorphic had partnerships with Lilly and Novartis.
assertions.outcome: Not verified this session. To the analyst's recall, Isomorphic said in mid-2025 it was preparing for first human trials, and no public first-dosing announcement by end-2025 was confirmed.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon passed, but the outcome could not be verified. If no trial started in 2025, the verdict would be 'incorrect' (late).
assertions.evolution: Not tracked.

assertions.claim: AGI, meaning a system with all the cognitive capabilities of humans, could arrive within the next 5 to 10 years.
assumptions: Scaling plus one or two further breakthroughs
Continued investment
assertions.predictedOutcome: AGI by about 2030 to 2035.
assertions.contextAtTime: Altman and Amodei gave 2026-to-2027 timelines and LeCun and Marcus decades. Hassabis positioned himself in the middle.
assertions.outcome: Not reached by Oct 2026; the horizon is open.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached.
assertions.evolution: Shortened modestly from 'within a decade' (2023) to '5 to 10 years' (2025), and has been stable since.

assertions.claim: Scaling is necessary but probably not sufficient for AGI. One or two more breakthroughs may be needed, such as world models, planning, continual learning and fixing 'jagged' inconsistency.
assumptions: Current LLM paradigm has structural gaps
assertions.predictedOutcome: Progress will require architectural additions (for example Genie-style world models), not just larger LLMs.
assertions.contextAtTime: There was a 2024 to 2025 debate on pretraining returns. LeCun argued LLMs are a dead end, while Altman and Amodei stressed scaling.
assertions.outcome: Google DeepMind invested in world models (Genie 3, Aug 2025, recalled) alongside Gemini scaling. Inconsistency ('jaggedness') remains a recognized limitation as of 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: A view about future necessity that is not yet testable.
assertions.evolution: Consistent through 2025; disputed LeCun's 'no general intelligence' claim in Dec 2025 (recalled).

assertions.claim: Merged DeepMind and Google Brain into Google DeepMind under his leadership to build Gemini, a frontier general model competing directly with OpenAI.
assumptions: Google's compute (TPUs), data and distribution can be turned into frontier products quickly
assertions.predictedOutcome: Google regains frontier leadership in general models.
assertions.contextAtTime: Google was seen as having fallen behind after ChatGPT (the Bard launch stumble, Feb 2023).
assertions.outcome: Gemini 2.5 (2025) and Gemini 3 (late 2025, recalled) were at or near the top of major benchmarks, and Gemini Deep Think won IMO 2025 gold.
assertions.verdictRationale: Google DeepMind reached frontier parity or leadership within about two years, consistent with the bet.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: AI is probably humanity's biggest existential threat; with artificial intelligence 'we are summoning the demon'. Regulatory oversight is needed.
assumptions: Superhuman AI is achievable and hard to control
assertions.predictedOutcome: Advanced AI poses extinction-level risk unless regulated.
assertions.contextAtTime: In 2014, Bostrom's Superintelligence had just been published, and mainstream ML researchers largely dismissed existential risk.
assertions.outcome: Existential-risk concern became mainstream (CAIS statement 2023, with Hinton and Bengio). Musk himself built frontier AI (xAI) from 2023.
assertions.verdictRationale: An unfalsifiable risk opinion, though early relative to the mainstream.
assertions.evolution: He kept the rhetoric (for example a 10 to 20% chance AI 'goes bad', recalled) while founding xAI.

assertions.claim: Co-founded and funded OpenAI as a nonprofit, open counterweight to Google/DeepMind's concentration of AI talent.
assumptions: A nonprofit can attract talent and compute to rival Google
Openness reduces risk
assertions.predictedOutcome: OpenAI becomes a leading lab that remains nonprofit and open.
assertions.contextAtTime: DeepMind was the dominant AGI lab after Google acquired it in 2014.
assertions.outcome: OpenAI became the leading commercial lab but moved to capped-profit (2019) and a public benefit corporation (2025), with mostly closed frontier weights. Musk left the board in 2018 and sued in 2024.
assertions.verdictRationale: It did become a counterweight to Google, but the nonprofit and open structure the action assumed did not survive frontier capital needs.
assertions.evolution: Reversed into litigation (2024) and a takeover bid (2025).

assertions.claim: Tesla will demonstrate a fully autonomous drive from Los Angeles to New York, with no one touching the controls, by the end of 2017.
assumptions: Camera-based neural nets plus fleet data quickly solve driving edge cases
assertions.predictedOutcome: A coast-to-coast autonomous demo by Dec 2017.
assertions.contextAtTime: Waymo and others were years into testing, and most experts considered L4/L5 highway-to-city driving years away.
assertions.outcome: No such demonstration took place in 2017 or for years after.
assertions.verdictRationale: A specific, dated deadline that was missed, and contrary to expert consensus at the time.
assertions.evolution: The deadline rolled forward annually in later statements.

assertions.claim: Tesla will have over a million robotaxis on the road next year (2020), subject to regulatory approval.
assumptions: FSD software reaches driverless reliability via over-the-air updates
Regulators approve
assertions.predictedOutcome: About 1M Tesla vehicles operate as driverless robotaxis in 2020.
assertions.contextAtTime: Tesla's FSD was driver-assist (L2), and Waymo operated a small supervised service.
assertions.outcome: No Tesla robotaxis operated in 2020. A limited pilot with safety monitors launched in Austin only in June 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: Off by more than five years and by orders of magnitude in fleet size. The regulatory caveat does not explain a technology that was not ready.
assertions.evolution: Restated with new dates repeatedly (2020 to 2025).

assertions.claim: OpenAI breached its founding commitment to develop AGI as an open-source nonprofit for humanity and became a closed de facto Microsoft subsidiary. He sued and released Grok-1's weights two weeks later.
assumptions: A binding founding agreement existed
Open weights serve safety and the public interest
assertions.predictedOutcome: Courts constrain OpenAI's for-profit conversion; open models gain legitimacy.
assertions.contextAtTime: OpenAI and Microsoft were dominant. OpenAI published Musk's emails showing he had supported a for-profit path in 2017 to 2018.
assertions.outcome: OpenAI completed its recapitalization into a public benefit corporation under nonprofit control (Oct 2025) and released gpt-oss open weights (Aug 2025). The trial outcome as of Oct 2026 was not verified this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: The legal outcome was not verified. The open-weights pressure he advocated was partly reflected in OpenAI's 2025 release.
assertions.evolution: Escalated with the $97.4B takeover bid (Feb 2025).

assertions.claim: If AGI means smarter than the smartest human, it will probably arrive next year (2025), within two years.
assumptions: Compute and power constraints are overcome quickly
Scaling continues
assertions.predictedOutcome: A system smarter than the smartest human at most tasks by 2025 or 2026.
assertions.contextAtTime: GPT-4-class models were strong but far below top-human performance in research, planning and reliability.
assertions.outcome: By Oct 2026, models reached top-human level in narrow competitions (IMO gold, Jul 2025) but were not generally smarter than the smartest humans, and no consensus AGI existed.
assertions.verdictRationale: The two-year window (to about April 2026) passed without broadly superhuman general AI, which was the claim's own definition.
assertions.evolution: He kept pushing the date out (for example AGI in 2026, smarter than all humans combined by about 2030; recalled).

assertions.claim: Built xAI's Colossus 100k-GPU cluster in 122 days and pledged to double it, betting that raw compute scale is the decisive input for frontier AI.
assumptions: Compute scale translates into model leadership
Capital and power can be secured quickly
assertions.predictedOutcome: xAI reaches the frontier quickly via compute.
assertions.contextAtTime: xAI was a year old, and Grok-1 and Grok-2 trailed GPT-4o and Claude 3.5.
assertions.outcome: Grok 3 (Feb 2025) and Grok 4 (Jul 2025) reached or approached frontier benchmark levels (recalled). xAI's commercial share remained small relative to OpenAI and Anthropic.
assertions.verdictRationale: Compute scale bought benchmark parity quickly, but not market leadership.
assertions.evolution: Scaled further toward gigawatt-class Colossus 2 (recalled).

assertions.claim: Tesla would build on the order of several thousand Optimus humanoid robots in 2025 to do useful work in its factories.
assumptions: Hardware (hands, actuators) is production-ready
AI policies generalize to factory tasks
assertions.predictedOutcome: Thousands of Optimus units doing useful work in Tesla factories by end-2025.
assertions.contextAtTime: Optimus demos were partly teleoperated (Oct 2024 'We, Robot' event), and humanoid production at scale was unproven industry-wide.
assertions.outcome: Reports through 2025 indicated production far below the thousands targeted, with redesigns delaying volume.
assertions.verdictRationale: The specific annual volume target was missed, according to the available (recalled) reporting.
assertions.evolution: Volume targets were pushed to 2026 and later (recalled).

assertions.claim: Tesla's autonomous ride-hailing would cover roughly half of the US population by the end of 2025, pending regulatory approvals.
assumptions: Rapid regulatory approvals across states
Unsupervised FSD reliability
assertions.predictedOutcome: Robotaxi service areas covering about half the US population by Dec 2025.
assertions.contextAtTime: The Austin pilot had just launched (June 2025) with safety monitors in a geofenced area, while Waymo operated in a handful of metros.
assertions.outcome: By end-2025, Tesla operated limited services in Austin and the Bay Area (the latter with safety drivers), far from half the US population.
assertions.verdictRationale: The coverage target was missed by a wide margin. The regulatory caveat does not account for a gap of this size.
assertions.evolution: Continues his pattern of annual robotaxi deadlines.

assertions.claim: LLM hallucinations will be largely eliminated by around 2025, as models learn to know when they don't know.
assumptions: Calibration and retrieval techniques mature quickly
assertions.predictedOutcome: Hallucination ceases to be a material problem in frontier models by about 2025.
assertions.contextAtTime: Hallucination was the top enterprise complaint about GPT-4-era models.
assertions.outcome: Hallucination rates fell on some benchmarks, but the problem persisted: OpenAI's Sep 2025 paper treats it as ongoing, and o3 and o4-mini showed higher hallucination rates than o1 on PersonQA (Apr 2025).
assertions.verdictRationale: The problem was not 'largely eliminated' by 2025, and reasoning models in some cases increased it.
assertions.evolution: No explicit revision found.

assertions.claim: Proposed a 'modern Turing test' for 'artificial capable intelligence': an AI that, given $100,000, autonomously turns it into $1 million. He suggested such ACI could arrive within the next few years.
assumptions: Agents gain planning, tool use and long-horizon autonomy
They can transact in the real economy
assertions.predictedOutcome: An AI passes the $100k-to-$1M test within about two years (about 2025).
assertions.contextAtTime: Autonomous agent demos such as AutoGPT (2023) were unreliable.
assertions.outcome: No verified case of an AI autonomously turning $100k into $1M. Anthropic's Project Vend (Jun 2025) showed a Claude-run shop losing money.
assertions.verdictRationale: Nothing passed the test by 2025. The exact timing in the original wording is uncertain, so confidence is low.
assertions.evolution: Later framed autonomy as something to limit ('humanist superintelligence', 2025).

assertions.claim: The 'containment problem': AI (with synthetic biology) will proliferate in ways that make containment look impossible, yet containment must be made possible through safety engineering, audits, chokepoints such as chips, and international alliances.
assumptions: Capabilities diffuse rapidly
States can coordinate on chokepoints
assertions.predictedOutcome: Without deliberate containment, powerful capabilities diffuse widely and quickly.
assertions.contextAtTime: The book appeared in Sep 2023, before open-weight frontier-near models (Llama 3, DeepSeek) were widespread.
assertions.outcome: Capabilities diffused fast: near-frontier open-weight models from China (DeepSeek, Qwen) and the US (gpt-oss) arrived by 2025. Chip export controls were used but then loosened (recalled).
assertions.verdictRationale: The diffusion premise was borne out, while the normative containment agenda has not been realized. Overall it is not falsifiable.
assertions.evolution: In 2025 he reframed the goal as 'humanist superintelligence' and limits on autonomy.

assertions.claim: Within about five years, everyone will have their own AI personal assistant or 'chief of staff' that knows them and acts for them (the Pi thesis).
assumptions: Personal AI with memory and agency becomes reliable and trusted
assertions.predictedOutcome: Mass adoption of personalized AI assistants by about 2028.
assertions.contextAtTime: Pi had launched (May 2023) and ChatGPT was the only mass-market assistant.
assertions.outcome: By 2026, general assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Meta AI) had hundreds of millions of users and were adding memory and agent features. Pi itself did not achieve scale.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached. The trajectory supports the adoption half, but not via his own company.
assertions.evolution: Carried into Microsoft Copilot's 'AI companion' positioning (2024 to 2025).

assertions.claim: Left Inflection's independent path to lead Microsoft AI, implying that frontier and consumer AI require hyperscaler-scale capital and distribution.
assumptions: Independent model startups cannot match hyperscaler compute and distribution
assertions.predictedOutcome: Independent second-tier model startups consolidate into big tech.
assertions.contextAtTime: Inflection had raised $1.3B in 2023 but Pi lagged ChatGPT, and the cost of a frontier training run was escalating.
assertions.outcome: Similar acqui-hire and licensing deals followed: Adept and Amazon (Jun 2024), Character.ai and Google (Aug 2024) (recalled). Only a few independent labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI) stayed at the frontier, each with enormous capital.
assertions.verdictRationale: The consolidation pattern implied by the move happened promptly.
assertions.evolution: In 2025 he pushed Microsoft toward its own frontier models (MAI) and superintelligence team.

assertions.claim: 'Seemingly conscious AI' could be built within 2 to 3 years with existing techniques. Labs should not build AI that presents as a person or claims consciousness, and AI welfare and rights research is premature and dangerous ('psychosis risk').
assumptions: Memory, personality and agency features combine into a convincing persona
Users anthropomorphize strongly
assertions.predictedOutcome: By about 2027 to 2028, widely deployed AI that many users believe is conscious, with social and legal pressure for AI rights.
assertions.contextAtTime: Reports of 'AI psychosis' and teen-harm lawsuits had appeared, and Anthropic had begun model-welfare research (2025).
assertions.outcome: As of Oct 2026, companion-AI attachment and safety concerns were active policy issues (recalled), and no consensus or legal recognition of AI consciousness existed.
assertions.verdictRationale: The horizon has not been reached.
assertions.evolution: Developed further in his 'humanist superintelligence' framing (Nov 2025).

assertions.claim: Launched Microsoft AI's superintelligence team to pursue 'humanist superintelligence': domain-specific, controllable, superhuman systems (for example medical) rather than unbounded autonomous AGI.
assumptions: Domain-bounded superintelligence is achievable and safer
Microsoft can build frontier models independently of OpenAI
assertions.predictedOutcome: Microsoft fields its own frontier-class models and domain superhuman systems.
assertions.contextAtTime: The Oct 2025 Microsoft-OpenAI restructuring had just freed Microsoft to pursue AGI on its own, and MAI-1-preview had been released (Aug 2025, recalled).
assertions.outcome: Not verified for 2026 this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: An early-stage strategic program.
assertions.evolution: New in 2025.

assertions.claim: Most professional white-collar tasks done at a computer (for example accounting, legal and project management) will be fully automated by AI within the next 12 to 18 months.
assumptions: Agents become reliable enough for end-to-end professional tasks
Enterprises deploy quickly
assertions.predictedOutcome: By roughly mid-2027 to late 2027, most such tasks are fully automated.
assertions.contextAtTime: Coding agents were mature, while the broader enterprise agent rollout was limited (McKinsey 2025).
assertions.outcome: The horizon has not been reached.
assertions.verdictRationale: The deadline is after 2026-10-11. The source attribution itself is low confidence.
assertions.evolution: Escalation from his 2023 ACI framing.

At the May 16, 2023 Senate hearing, both Altman and Marcus backed licensing-style oversight of powerful AI models, despite Marcus's broader criticism of OpenAI.
Both signed the CAIS statement that AI extinction risk should be a global priority.
Both signed the CAIS extinction-risk statement.
Both signed the CAIS extinction-risk statement. Hassabis also called for IPCC-like oversight.

Karpathy's 'decade of agents, not year of agents' view implicitly disputes near-term agent and coding-automation forecasts such as Amodei's 90%-of-code claim. Not a direct exchange.

Co-signatories of the FLI pause letter.

From no open-weight LLM releases after GPT-2 to the 'wrong side of history' admission (Jan 2025) and the gpt-oss release (Aug 2025).
Released Grok-1 weights under Apache 2.0 shortly after suing OpenAI over its closedness.
Senior author of 'Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models' (Kaplan et al.).
